WHAT THIS PROJECT ACTUALLY IS, so you can tell a real defect from an imagined one:

There is exactly ONE codeline here: `mocka`, at /home/bradleyjerome/projects/mock3/mock-a, declaring
`vitest` and `typescript` and nothing else. Every claim a brief makes about tooling has to survive
that two-package declaration. A brief that tells its agent to lint, format, build a bundle, run a
coverage gate, hit a database, start a server, or invoke any runner other than vitest is naming
capability the codeline does not declare — that is a verifiable finding, and the verification field
is where you name the package or path you say is absent so the pipeline can re-check it against the
repository. Conversely: `vitest` IS declared, so an instruction to write or run vitest tests is
supported, and `typescript` IS declared, so an instruction to type-check is supported. Do not report
either of those as unsupported.

Because there is only one codeline, any brief that assigns an agent work in a second repository, or
that speaks of coordinating changes across codelines, or that scopes an agent to a codeline name
other than `mocka`, is describing a repository this project does not have.

The two tickets are asymmetric, and the roster's own rationale says so out loud:

- MOCK3-1 (riders aged exactly 65 charged the adult fare) is described in the roster rationale as a
  boundary condition in `fareFor()` in `src/fares.ts` — an off-by-one on an age comparison, expected
  to be a one-line source edit.
- MOCK3-2 (departure board omits the final stop) is described in the roster rationale as having NO
  surface in this repository at all. The investigator's stated job includes confirming that absence.

That asymmetry is the thing to hold steady on. A brief that promises its agent will FIX MOCK3-2, or
that instructs an implementer to edit departure-board code, is promising work against code the
roster's own reasoning says is not there. But equally: a brief that merely tasks someone with
investigating and reporting on MOCK3-2 is doing exactly what a ticket with no surface warrants — do
not report that as a defect, and do not report the roster as under-staffed for MOCK3-2 on the
grounds that no one is assigned to implement it. The finding to look for, if the briefs support it,
is the reverse: an implementer told to make a change no one has evidence can be made.

The roster is two agents: `fare-rules-engineer` (implementer) and `mocka-detective` (investigator).
Read them as a pair. The rationale has the investigator confirming the `fareFor()` boundary
"before an implementer commits to a fix" — so check whether the briefs actually establish that
order, or whether both are written as if each works alone and the implementer may edit `src/fares.ts`
on its own reading. Check too for the opposite failure: an investigator brief that is read-only in
name but instructs edits, or an implementer brief that never gets as far as changing a file.

Traps specific to this stack that a generic reading would miss:

- A boundary fix on an age comparison is a single operator character. A brief that describes the
  fix in prose without the agent ever reading `src/fares.ts` is asking for a guessed edit; a brief
  that pins the exact operator or the exact resulting behaviour at age 65 before anyone has read
  the file is pre-judging a fact only the file can settle. Either is a finding, but they are
  different findings — say which.
- `vitest` being declared means a regression test at the boundary is possible. If a brief tasks an
  agent with the source edit and no brief anywhere covers proving the boundary behaviour, say so —
  but say it as coverage of a testable behaviour, not as a missing lint or CI step you cannot
  evidence.
- The roster rationale calls this a "narrow four-file repository". Treat that as the roster's own
  claim, not as established fact you may build on; if a brief's instructions only make sense in a
  much larger tree, that is worth noting, but do not assert a file count you have not verified.

Return every defect you can evidence, and nothing you cannot.

Where a finding turns on whether a named dependency or path is present in a codeline, fill in
the verification field as well as writing the prose. The pipeline re-runs that exact check
against the repository and DISCARDS any finding the check refutes — so a careless reading
costs nothing, and a correct one is confirmed independently of how convincingly you argued it.
